story_text:
The first drops were fat and slow, each one landing on the harbor planks with a sound like a knuckle on a door. Eren heard them before he felt them. He stood on the quay with a coil of wet hemp over his shoulder and watched the sky over the water turn the color of an old bruise. Out past the moorings the sea had stopped rolling and started heaving, gathering itself in long gray muscles. The storm had begun, and nobody in the harbor had any doubt about it anymore.

He worked fast. The little blue trawler first, because its owner was in town and would never forgive a scraped hull. Then the two dinghies, then the fat-bellied cutter that always strained at its lines like a dog that wanted to chase something. He doubled every knot. He had learned from the old net-menders that a knot you trust is a knot you have not tested, and that the sea tests everything. The wind came in sideways now, and the rain stopped being drops and became a thrown handful of gravel. His fingers went numb and clumsy. The last line, the stern line of the cutter, snapped taut as he hauled it and dragged through his palms. It burned a red stripe into each hand. He swore, laughed at himself for swearing at a rope, and threw a final hitch over the bollard, leaning his whole weight on it until it bit and held.

That should have been the end of it. The harbor shed had a stove and a kettle and a bench worn smooth by a hundred waiting backsides. Anyone with sense would have ducked in there, shut the door and let the night go howling past.

Eren did not go to the shed. He stood at the end of the quay with his collar clutched shut and his stinging hands tucked under his arms, and he looked out along the breakwater to where the lighthouse stood against the dark. It was a stubby, stained tower at the very tip of the long stone arm, and as far as he could remember it had never once been lit. He had lived beside it all his life and had never set foot inside. It had simply been there, like a locked drawer in a familiar house.

Why was it in his head tonight, of all nights? He turned the question over while the rain ran off his nose. He had tied the last knot. He had done what he came to do. Yet some stubborn corner of his mind kept tugging, like a loose thread on a sleeve, toward that dark tower. He did not yet know what the thread was attached to. He only knew that, standing there with the storm leaning on his shoulders, he was more curious than afraid, and that surprised him.

Then he remembered.

It had been old Salih, two winters ago, mending a net on the shed bench with a pipe clamped in his teeth. Salih had not looked up. He had said, in the flat voice he used for things he considered unimportant, that there was a letter in the lighthouse. It was tucked behind the brass plate of the lamp-room door, he said, and had been there longer than anyone cared to count. Nobody had touched it. Eren had asked whose it was, and Salih had only shrugged around his pipe stem. "Somebody who wanted it kept," he said. "Or somebody who wanted it found. Hard to tell with letters." Then he had gone back to his net, and Eren had gone back to his work, and the thing had sunk out of sight like a stone in a pond.

Now it rose again, whole and dripping.

He stood there for a long time, weighing it. A letter left in a tower no one visited. A storm that would batter that tower from every side. A door whose latch, he had heard, was rusted and rattled in every wind. Salih had said nobody had touched it, but nobody had been looking, either. Tonight the tide would climb over parts of the breakwater. Tonight the wind would wrench at that old door. If the latch gave, if the rain got in, if some drifter or some bored boy wandered up the stones tomorrow and found paper that was never meant for him, then whatever it said would belong to everyone and no one.

The shed was warm. The shed was twenty steps behind him.

Eren turned his back on it, pulled his cap down to his eyebrows and stepped onto the breakwater.

The stones were slick as fish skin. The wind hit him in the ribs and tried to shoulder him off the edge, and on his left the sea came up in black walls and fell apart against the rocks, throwing cold spray that tasted of iron. His montu was soaked through within a hundred paces, heavy as a wet sail. He walked bent over, one hand brushing the stones for balance, counting steps to keep his fear in order. Behind him the harbor lamps shrank to a few smudged yellow points. Ahead, the tower grew out of the dark, stained and enormous. He had walked past it a thousand times in daylight, and now that he was about to enter it, it felt like a stranger.

He did not know what lay inside. That was the odd part. He knew every plank of the quay, every cleat and ringbolt, but he could not have said whether the tower held one room or ten, whether the stairs wound left or right, whether the floor was stone or boards. He was walking toward a place he could only guess at. The thought should have slowed him down. It hurried him instead.

The door was a slab of black wood bound with iron, and the wind had already pried it a hand's width open. Eren put his shoulder to it. It groaned, resisted, then swung inward all at once and let him stumble into a darkness that smelled of salt, cold stone and long-dead lamp oil. He dragged the door shut behind him, and the roar of the storm dropped to a muffled drumming, as though the whole night had been moved into the next room.

He stood dripping, waiting for his eyes to learn the dark. Gradually a few things came out of it. A circular wall, rough and sweating. A spiral stair of iron, climbing out of sight. A stub of candle in a tin dish on the floor, left by someone who might have been gone a year or ten. He had matches in his breast pocket, wrapped in a scrap of oilcloth out of old habit, and the third one caught. The candle flame fattened, shivered and steadied.

He climbed.

The stair rang under his boots, and each ring seemed too loud, as if the tower disapproved. Round and round he went, past slit windows where the storm threw its fists against the glass, until his thighs burned and his breath turned ragged. At the top the stair ended at a small door, and on that door, just as Salih had said, was a tarnished brass plate. One corner of a pale envelope showed behind it.

He had expected a thrill. What he felt instead was a cold, careful quiet. He drew the envelope out with two fingers, slowly, the way one lifts something from a sleeping animal. It was damp. The roof or the walls had been weeping onto it for who knew how long, and the paper had gone soft, its edges curling like the petals of a dying flower. On the front there was no name. Only a smudge where a name might once have been.

His thumb found the flap. It was not sealed anymore. It would open with the least pressure.

He did not open it.

He stood there in the little round antechamber with the candle guttering in his other hand and made himself think. Whose was it? It had not been written to him, that much was certain. It had not been written by him, either. Somebody had stood where he was standing, maybe on a night like this one, and slid it behind that plate and walked away. Why there? Why not carry it down to the harbor, or burn it, or mail it? Because the writer could not deliver it? Because the writer would not? Because the person it was meant for was supposed to come here, and had not? Every possibility had a different face, and none of the faces would turn toward him.

The envelope was wet through. If he forced the pages apart now, he could tear them, and a torn letter was worse than an unread one. So he did the only sensible thing. He set the candle on the top step and lowered himself to sit beside it, with the soft envelope held flat on his knee, close enough to the flame to be warmed and far enough not to scorch. He would wait for it to dry. Outside, the storm leaned on the tower, and the tower, patient and stained, leaned back.

He was cold, and he had a great deal of time to think. He thought of Salih and his flat voice. He thought of the ropes he had tied, each knot a little promise to the boats. He thought of the red stripes across his palms, which had begun to throb now that he was still. After a long while, he realized he had stopped counting minutes. The paper had stopped steaming. It had stiffened at the edges and gone from the color of wet ash to the color of weak tea.

He turned the envelope over twice. Then, finally, he said aloud, to nobody, "I'm sorry. I think this is wrong. I think I'm going to do it anyway."

He knew it was a violation. Somebody might have meant this for one pair of eyes only, and his were not those eyes. But he also knew that if he folded it back behind the plate and walked down into the storm, he would carry the unopened thing in his head for the rest of his life, and that kind of silence seemed to him worse than a trespass. He drew out the pages.

There were two of them, covered in a narrow slanting hand, the ink blurred in places by water but mostly alive. He tilted them to the candle and read.

The first lines were not what he expected. There was no greeting, no name, no confession. They began in the middle of a thought, as if the writer had been speaking for a long time before reaching for a pen. The writer spoke of this tower, of the long dark nights when the water around it turned treacherous, and of the boats that came home along the line of the breakwater trusting that someone, somewhere, had left a light for them. The writer admitted to being tired. The writer admitted to being afraid of being forgotten. Then the hand grew firmer, the words pressed deeper into the paper, and the last paragraph said what the whole letter had been built to say: when the storm comes, whoever finds this, do not let the light go out. Keep it burning. Whatever else you do or do not understand, keep it burning until the sea lies down.

He turned the page over to find the signature. There was one. Or there had been. At the bottom a long wet bloom of ink had spread across the paper, swallowing the letters until they were no more than a gray cloud. He held it close to the flame. He tilted it. He squinted until his eyes watered. He could not tell whether the first letter had been an A or an H, whether the name was long or short, whether it belonged to a man or a woman or a child. Whoever had written this had been washed out of their own letter.

Eren sat back against the cold stone and let the pages rest in his lap. The storm hammered on. Somewhere below him the iron stair gave a soft metallic tick as the tower flexed in the wind.

"Who are you?" he said, and his voice sounded small and strange in the round room.

No answer came, of course. But he found that he was no longer curious in the way he had been on the quay, restless and itching. The question had changed shape. It was not who wrote this that pressed on him anymore, but who was supposed to do what it asked. He had not been named, but he was the one holding the paper.

He was exhausted. His arms shook from the climb and the cold, his hands burned, and the harbor shed with its stove and its kettle was a long, wet walk away. Any reasonable person would have gone back down, folded the letter into an inner pocket, and let the storm do what storms do. The owner could be hunted for in daylight. The letter had waited this long, after all.

But the sea would not wait until daylight, and somewhere out there, on the black water beyond the glass, might be a boat that was not tied to any bollard.

He pushed open the small door at the top of the stair.

The lamp room was a glass cage perched on the roof of the tower, and the storm struck it from every side at once, rattling the panes in their frames. In the middle stood the great lamp, a thing of brass and old lenses, furred with dust. He circled it slowly, holding up the candle, and found the reservoir, the wick, and a rusted can of oil on a shelf beneath the sill. Nobody had told him how to do this. The letter did not explain. He did it the way he had learned everything on the harbor, by looking at what was in front of him and asking what it wanted. He trimmed the wick with his pocketknife. He filled the reservoir with unsteady hands, spilling some, wiping it on his sleeve. He touched the candle to the wick.

Nothing. Then a blue bead, then a hesitant yellow tongue, then a sudden steady flame that swelled behind the lenses and threw itself outward. The glass room filled with gold. A bar of light swept across the rain, lit the heaving back of the sea, and stretched all the way to the harbor, where the smudged lamps seemed suddenly small and far away.

Eren stood with his mouth slightly open. Then he laughed, short and breathless, and pressed a hand to the warm brass.

The storm did not care. It battered the glass and shrieked in the gaps of the frame, and the flame bent and flinched in its chimney. He understood quickly that lighting it had been the easy part. It needed watching. The wick would burn down, the oil would drain, the draft would try to snuff it. Every few minutes he had to adjust, top up and shield it with his body. He pulled a stool over, sat down beside the lamp with the letter held in both hands, and began to keep his watch.

He did not know whose light this was supposed to be. He did not know who had stood here before him, or whether that person was still alive, or whether they would ever walk up the stair to ask what he had done with their words. Those questions would have to wait for morning, if morning came. All he had for certain was the flame, the letter, the rope-burn across his palms and the long gold arm of light reaching out of the tower into the dark, toward the boats he had tied and any he had not.

The wind rose and the rain thickened. He leaned in close to the lamp and cupped his hand around the flame, and the faded gray cloud where a name should have been lay quietly in his lap while the night went on.
